prompt.context: Your client is a craft beer company called Duck Island Beer Company out of Austin, TX. They are an international craft beer company beloved by craft drinkers around the world. They are looking to start selling beer in the United Kingdom. They want to know which style of beer to sell and if it would be profitable.
prompt.question: Which style of beer should Duck Island sell in the UK, and would entering the UK market be profitable?

clarifying_info.q: What is Duck Island's current market share?
clarifying_info.a: See Exhibit 1 — Duck Island holds 39% global market share, the largest of any single company.

clarifying_info.q: What are Duck Island's current financials?

clarifying_info.a: Over 50 brands split between lagers, ales, IPAs, and stouts.
Seeking rapid expansion and revenue in any way possible.

clarifying_info.q: Where does Duck Island currently operate?
clarifying_info.a: Everywhere in the world except the UK, Africa, and Australia.

clarifying_info.q: Is the UK a good craft beer market?
clarifying_info.a: The UK shows potential as a craft market.

exhibits.title: Global Market Share
exhibits.shows: Pie chart of global beer market share by company
exhibits.data: Duck Island 39%, Smith Cools 35%, Hammerstein 12%, Star Beer 7%, ~100 Companies 7%

exhibits.title: Beer Market in UK
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing total number of brands and number of competitors by beer style in the UK market
exhibits.data: Styles shown: Lager, Ale, India Pale Ale, Stout. Two bars per style: Brands and Competitors. Lager and Ale have the most brands and competitors; IPA has the fewest brands and competitors (approximately 5 brands, 2–3 competitors); Stout is mid-range.

exhibits.shows: Four separate line charts (2013–2016) showing sales trends in USD millions for each beer style: Ales, IPAs, Lagers, Stouts
exhibits.data: Ales: ~$8M in 2013, relatively flat to ~$8M in 2016; IPAs: ~$0.5M in 2013, rising steeply to ~$3.5M in 2016; Lagers: ~$10M in 2013, relatively flat ~$10M in 2016; Stouts: ~$8M in 2013, roughly flat to ~$9M in 2016

framework: External / Market factors: size and growth of UK craft beer market, consumer demand by style, regulatory and tariff environment, competitive landscape and barriers to entry
Revenue: pricing strategy, volume estimates, product mix (which style)
Costs: variable costs (brewing, raw materials, packaging), fixed costs, shipping/logistics, tariffs, CapEx if building local brewery
Market entry mode: export from US vs. brew locally in UK vs. acquisition/JV
Strategic fit: alignment with Duck Island's rapid-expansion strategy, brand positioning as craft/US import

questions.prompt: Based on the exhibits, which beer style should Duck Island enter the UK with, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should synthesize Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3 together. Exhibit 2 shows IPA has the fewest competing brands and competitors — lowest competitive intensity. Exhibit 3 shows IPA has the steepest sales growth trajectory 2013–2016. A strong candidate connects low competition with rising demand and recommends IPA. They may also note Duck Island's large global market share (Exhibit 1) gives it brand leverage and distribution power.

questions.prompt: What factors would influence the decision to enter the UK market? (Brainstorm)
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm in a MECE fashion. See brainstorming section for full expected categories and ideas.

questions.prompt: Duck Island wants to launch the 'Duck Island IPA.' Compare two entry methods: (1) Brew in the US and export to the UK, vs. (2) Brew locally in the UK and brand it as a US Beer. Which do you recommend and why? Calculate the profitability of each option given: Estimated sales = 2,000 barrels in year 1; Price = $10 per 6-pack; 165 12-oz bottles per half-barrel (so 330 bottles per full barrel). Imported from US: cost of brewing = $0.50/bottle, cost of shipping = $0.50/bottle, tariff = $1 per 6-pack. Brewed in UK: cost of brewing = $0.50/bottle, cost of shipping = $0.50/bottle, no tariffs, CapEx for new brewery = $110,000.
questions.guidance: Candidate should work through the math for both scenarios, arrive at equal Year 1 profit of $330,000, and then make a qualitative recommendation. A strong candidate notes that the US-brew option benefits from 'imported US beer' brand cachet, while the UK-brew option has lower ongoing costs after the first-year CapEx is recovered, making it more profitable in Year 2+.

math.setup: Step 1: Total bottles. Each barrel = 2 half-barrels, each half-barrel = 165 bottles, so each barrel = 330 bottles. 2,000 barrels x 330 bottles/barrel = 660,000 bottles. Step 2: Revenue. 660,000 bottles / 6 bottles per 6-pack = 110,000 six-packs. 110,000 x $10 = $1,100,000. Step 3a (Import): Total cost = (brewing + shipping + tariff per bottle) x bottles = ($0.50 + $0.50 + $1/6) x 660,000 = ($1.00 + $0.1667) x 660,000 = $1.1667 x 660,000 ≈ $770,000. Step 3b (UK brew): Total cost = (brewing + shipping) x bottles + CapEx = ($0.50 + $0.50) x 660,000 + $110,000 = $660,000 + $110,000 = $770,000. Step 4: Profit both cases = $1,100,000 - $770,000 = $330,000.
steps: Total bottles = 2,000 barrels x (165 x 2) bottles/barrel = 660,000 bottles
math.answer: $330,000 profit in Year 1 for both options. From Year 2 onward, UK brewing is more profitable because CapEx is a one-time cost.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would influence Duck Island's decision to enter the UK market?

categories.name: Internal
ideas: Cash on hand for CapEx investment
Knowledge of the UK market and consumer preferences
Marketing strategy and brand positioning for a new geography
Existing supply chain capacity to support exports

categories.name: External — Competition & Market
ideas: Number and strength of existing craft beer competitors in the UK
Barriers to entry (distribution lock-in, shelf space, licensing)
Market share potential and realistic volume forecasts
Distribution channel availability (pubs, supermarkets, specialty retailers)

categories.name: External — Regulatory & Legal
ideas: Tariffs on imported alcohol
UK food and beverage regulations and labeling requirements
Legal drinking age and advertising restrictions in UK
Brexit implications for tariffs and trade rules
Currency volatility: USD to GBP conversion risk

categories.name: External — Operational
ideas: Shipping costs if brewed in the US
Cost differential of brewing locally in the UK
Supply chain extension costs (hops, bottles, packaging)
Temperature control and quality assurance during transport

categories.name: Cultural & Strategic
ideas: Converting a traditional ale/lager culture toward craft/IPA
Brand positioning as a US import vs. locally brewed
Timing relative to IPA growth trend in the UK
Alignment with Duck Island's rapid-expansion strategy

recommendation: Recommend that Duck Island enter the UK market by launching the Duck Island IPA, targeting a style with growing demand and low competitive intensity.

Both entry methods (US export and UK local brewing) yield equal Year 1 profit of $330,000, so the choice depends on strategic priorities: US brewing preserves brand authenticity as an imported craft beer; UK brewing offers greater profitability from Year 2 onward as the one-time $110,000 CapEx is absorbed.
Given the rapid-expansion strategy and IPA's favorable growth trajectory, entry is recommended.
risks: Brand risk if UK local brew is perceived as less authentic than a US import
Currency volatility (USD/GBP) could erode margins on the import model
Tariff changes post-Brexit could significantly raise import costs
Consumer adoption risk — converting traditional UK drinkers to craft IPA takes time and marketing investment
Competitive response from incumbent players if IPA category grows
next_steps: Conduct consumer research in the UK to validate IPA demand and test Duck Island brand recognition
Finalize entry mode decision based on brand strategy and 3-year financial model (import vs. local)
Identify distribution partners — pubs, supermarkets, specialty retailers
Develop UK-specific marketing campaign positioning Duck Island IPA
Monitor Brexit regulatory developments that may affect tariffs and trade
